analytic.title: Mixed-Criticality Scheduling on Multiprocessors with Service Guarantees

abstract.div:
Mixed-criticality (MC)
systems are composed of tasks with varying criticality co-hosted on a single shared platform. In conventional MC systems, upon criticality change, the lower criticality tasks are penalized to guarantee resources for the higher criticality ones. However, in practice, penalizing lower criticality tasks have adverse effects and hence, the system is often under-utilized. In this paper, we consider the problem of reservation-based scheduling of mixed-criticality systems on a homogeneous multiprocessor platform to guarantee full service to the lower criticality tasks when one of the processors switches to the critical state. We explore the semi-partitioned scheduling model for dual-criticality systems in which the low criticality tasks executing on a processor are migrated to another processor upon mode switch to improve the service offered to them in the high criticality mode. We present the scheduling strategy of the proposed algorithm and derive its utilization bound. To evaluate the proposed algorithm, we use randomly generated task sets to compare the schedulability performance of the algorithm with the existing algorithms. Our results show that the proposed algorithm improves both schedulability and low criticality support when compared to existing algorithms for implicit-deadline task systems.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Consolidating multiple applications with varying criticality (designated based on consequences of failure) onto a common hardware is a recent trend in safety-critical real-time systems. Mixed-Criticality (MC) task model was proposed to provide guaranteed execution and safe isolation for the critical components from the non-critical ones and to improve the overall system utilization. MC scheduling has received a growing attention in the real-time systems community in the recent past. See [1] for a comprehensive survey on MC scheduling algorithms.

Several MC scheduling algorithms that are efficient either in terms of scheduling a large class of task systems or in terms of theoretical bounds such as speed-up factor for both uniprocessor and multiprocessor systems have been designed in the past. Most of the previous works guarantee only the schedulability of high criticality tasks in the critical mode at the cost of low criticality tasks. Specifically, upon mode switch, the low criticality tasks are completely dropped in the system to meet the demand of the high criticality tasks. However, this method seriously impacts the performance which may not be suitable for many practical systems that require minimum service guarantee to these tasks [2], [5].

To overcome this problem several techniques have been proposed in the past such as reduced execution budget model wherein the low criticality tasks execute with reduced execution budget in the critical mode [2]- [4], increased period model (or elastic task model) where the low criticality tasks execute at a lower rate by extending their period/deadline in the critical mode [5], [6] and selective degradation model where the service is offered only to a subset of low criticality tasks depending on the available budget in the critical mode [7]- [9]. Although this problem has been well studied for the uniprocessor case, for multiprocessors there has been very little work.

Most multiprocessor MC algorithms are designed based on either global or partitioned scheduling. Under global MC scheduling when any of the high criticality tasks in a processor overruns its budget, then every processor in the system is switched to the critical mode. In the case of partitioned MC scheduling, all the tasks are statically mapped to a processor. As a result, they are not allowed to migrate at run-time during its execution. Thus, when a high criticality task executing on a processor overruns its budget, only that particular processor is switched to the critical mode.

In a partitioned dual-criticality system, there are tasks with two criticality levels. The high criticality tasks have two execution budgets based on the criticality level of the system and their execution budget increases with the criticality level. Upon a mode switch, the high criticality tasks require additional demand. To satisfy this demand, the low criticality tasks are penalized on that processor. Since the mode switch is local to that processor, these low criticality tasks instead of being discarded can be migrated to another processor which has not experienced mode switch. Hence, we propose a semi-partitioned strategy for dual-criticality systems that allow migration of low criticality tasks after the mode switch.

In this paper, we propose a reservation-based MC scheduling algorithm to guarantee full service to the low criticality tasks when one of the processors switches to the high criticality mode motivated by the following observation. The probability that a high criticality task overruns its budget is very low and degrading the service to the low criticality tasks if one such event occurs is very pessimistic. We consider a restricted migration model wherein only the low criticality tasks are allowed to migrate after mode switch. To keep the predictability of the high criticality task executions intact we do not allow them to migrate. The utilization corresponding to the migrating low criticality tasks is reserved in the processor to which it migrates. If the destination processor (to which it migrated) switches to high criticality mode, then these tasks will be discarded. We use the Earliest Deadline First with Virtual Deadlines (EDF-VD) algorithm for scheduling the tasks as it has an optimal speed-up bound [10].

We conducted experiments to evaluate the proposed scheduling algorithm and compared it with the existing algorithms. For implicit-deadline task systems, the schedulability improvement using our algorithm is as much as 24.3% when compared to existing algorithms. We also observed that our algorithm improves the low criticality support by as much as 29.2% when all the processors switch mode.

Related Work. There have been few studies on service guarantee scheme for multiprocessor MC systems. Su et al. [11] extended the uniprocessor elastic task model [5] for partitioned EDF scheduling. Ren et al. [12] presented a task grouping scheme for partitioned MC scheduling that can isolate different task groups by restricting the impact of mode switch within that group. Only the low criticality tasks executing in that group are suspended to guarantee resources for the high criticality tasks. Pathan [13] extended the imprecise MC model [3] with the quality of service values for the low criticality tasks and presented a fluid-based scheduling algorithm for the proposed model. None of the above work considers full service for the low criticality tasks (with their actual budget) after the mode switch.

There have been numerous studies on semi-partitioned scheduling algorithms in the non-MC domain. On the contrary, there are very few studies for MC systems. Burns et al. [14] proposed a semi-partitioned scheduling of cyclic executives for mixed-criticality systems. Awan et al. [15] extended the non-MC semi-partitioned algorithms for MC systems. However, their work did not consider service guarantee for the low criticality tasks in the high criticality mode.

There have been few studies on semi-partitioned MC scheduling with service guarantees. Zaid et al. [16] introduced a dual-partitioned scheduling model for dual-criticality task systems. In their model, the high criticality tasks are statically mapped to a processor, and the low critical tasks in a processor are migrated upon mode switch under the assumption that all the processors switch mode simultaneously. Their model assumes a fixed-partition for each of the criticality modes and hence the name dual-partitioned scheduling. However, their model did not consider the schedulability during the mode switch transition. Further, the low criticality tasks active during the mode switch are dropped and these tasks execute at a lower rate in the destination processor after the mode switch. Xu et al. [17] considered a semi-partitioned model for a dual-core system based on response time analysis [18] which allows the low criticality tasks to continue execution upon mode switch by completely migrating them to the other processor which has not experienced the mode switch. This model guarantees full service to the low criticality tasks when any one of the processors switches mode. If both processors switch mode, then all the low criticality tasks in the processor that switched mode last are dropped to meet the demand of the high criticality tasks on both these processors. Recently, Xu [19] extended this work to more than two processors where a low criticality task is allowed to migrate more than once and explored different semi-partitioning strategies.
In contrast to above studies, in this paper, we study the semi-partitioned reservation-based scheduling for guaranteeing full service to the low criticality tasks after one mode switch.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND A. System model
div.p: Mixed-Criticality (MC) scheduling problem is considered for a dual-criticality system scheduled on a multiprocessor platform with m identical unit-capacity processors. We consider a sporadic task set τ comprising of n tasks. Each MC task τ i is characterized by a tupule (T i ,χ i ,C L i ,C H i ), where T i is the minimum inter-arrival time (also called period), χ i ∈ {LC, HC} is the criticality level of the task (namely low criticality (LC) and high criticality (HC)), C L i is the LC execution budget, C H i is the HC execution budget. We assume 0 < C L i ≤ C H i ≤ T i for each HC task. Each task τ i has a relative deadline equal to T i .
LC task set τ L and HC task set τ H are defined as τ
div.formula: L def = {τ i ∈ τ | X i = LC} and τ H def = {τ i ∈ τ | X i = HC}.
div.p: LC and HC utilization of a task is defined as
div.formula: u L i def = C L i /T i and u H i def = C H i /T i respectively. Normalized system-level utilizations are defined as U L L def = τi∈τL u L i /m, U L H def = τi∈τH u L i /m, U H H def = τi∈τH u H i /m. System behavior:
div.p: System mode is a system-wide variable that represents the change in criticality level of the system. The system is said to be either in the LC or in the HC mode. The system is said to be in the LC mode if all tasks τ i ∈ τ signal completion within its LC execution budget and the system is said to be in the HC mode if any of the HC tasks τ i ∈ τ H executes beyond its LC execution budget but signals completion before its HC execution budget. The mode switch is defined as the first time instant at which any of the HC tasks execute beyond its LC execution during the LC mode. To meet the demand of HC tasks after mode switch, the scheduling algorithm will immediately migrate/discard the LC tasks.

div.head: B. EDF-VD Algorithm
div.p: Under the EDF-VD, each HC task is assigned a virtual deadline (D L i ) in the LC mode based on a single scaling factor x ∈ (0, 1), that is, [10]. These virtual deadlines are determined by uniformly distributing the LC mode slack among all the HC tasks. In the LC mode, LC tasks are scheduled using their actual deadline and HC tasks are scheduled using their virtual deadline. Upon a mode switch all the LC tasks are dropped and from thereon the HC tasks are scheduled using their actual deadline.
div.formula: D L i = x • T i

div.head: III. SEMI-PARTITIONED MIXED-CRITICALITY (SPMC)
div.p: In this section, we present our Semi-Partitioned Mixed-Criticality (SPMC) model to guarantee service to the LC tasks in the HC mode. We assume the cost of migration, preemption and cache-related overheads are negligible in our analysis and included when computing the execution budget of the tasks.

Execution Semantics. In the LC mode, all tasks are assigned to a dedicated processor. Each processor has a set of statically partitioned HC tasks, a set of statically partitioned LC tasks and a set of migrating LC tasks. If the processor switches to the HC mode, then the migrating LC tasks are To guarantee resources in the destination processor, the utilization corresponding to the migrating LC tasks is reserved in the LC mode. If both the dedicated and the destination processor switches to the HC mode then the migrating tasks in both these processors are dropped.

The scheduling strategy of SPMC is shown in Figure 1. The migrating LC tasks are modelled as a server with a budget and period. Each processor has two servers in the LC mode corresponding to the migrating LC tasks -incoming migration (IM ) and outgoing migration (OM ). After the mode switch, the servers are dropped and only the non-migrating LC tasks and HC tasks are active in the processor.

Let φ k denote the k th processor. Then the corresponding system utilization is given by U L L (φ k ), U L H (φ k ) and U H H (φ k ). We use τ (φ k ) to denote the set of tasks assigned to φ k . Let τ NM (φ k ), τ OM (φ k ) and τ IM (φ k ) denote the set of non-migrating, outgoing migrating and incoming migrating LC tasks respectively. Then U L L (φ k ) can be represented as
div.formula: U L OM (φ k ) + U L NM (φ k ) + U L IM (φ k ), where U L OM (φ k ) = τi∈τOM (φk) u L

div.head: C. Task Allocation
div.p: This section will describe how to allocate tasks to processors under SPMC. First, we try the non-migration approach (worstcase reservation) using decreasing utilization first-fit allocation. The semi-partitioned approach will only be applied if the non-migration approach fails. The detailed task allocation strategy of the SPMC algorithm is as follows:
1) The task set is first sorted based on their criticality and then based on their respective utilization,
div.formula: u H i if τ i ∈ τ H and u L i if τ i ∈ τ L .
div.p: 2) First, all the heavy tasks (those with utilization greater than the utilization bound) are assigned to a dedicated processor. If the number of heavy tasks is greater than the number of processors then the task system will be deemed unschedulable. 3) Then, all HC tasks are assigned to a dedicated processor using UDP allocation [21] (i.e., worst-fit on
div.formula: U H H (φ k ) - U L H (φ k )).
div.p: To enable reservation later, the HC tasks are assigned to a processor until the utilization bound on that processor is not violated. 4) Once all processors have been checked and if neither of them can schedule the HC task, then the task system will be deemed unschedulable. 5) When all HC tasks are assigned to processors, the LC tasks are considered for assignment using UDP allocation. 6) A LC task is assigned to a dedicated processor (as nonmigrating task) if it can execute in the HC mode on the same processor such that the utilization bound condition is not violated. Otherwise, the task will be marked as migrating LC task. Note that the non-migrating LC tasks are treated like HC tasks. 7) Then, the migrating LC tasks will be considered for assignment using worst-fit allocation based on total utilization in LC mode (U L L (φ k ) + U L H (φ k )). 8) The migrating LC task will be allocated to a pair of processors -one dedicated processor in the LC mode and another processor for migration if the dedicated processor switches to the HC mode. The migrating LC task is said to be allocated only if it is schedulable in both the processors. 9) If the migrating LC task cannot be allocated to any of the processors, then the task system is said to be unschedulable.

V. EXPERIMENTS In this section, we evaluate the schedulability performance of SPMC algorithm using the randomly generated task sets and compare it with the existing scheduling algorithms that can tolerate one mode switch instant. The algorithms include Semi-FP [17] and WCR-EDF.

• Semi-FP is a fixed-priority based semi-partitioned scheduling algorithm for dual-core systems. At the mode switch, the algorithm migrates the LC tasks from one processor to another. It uses criticality-aware partitioning with worst-fit allocation based on the utilization values at their respective criticality levels. • WCR-EDF is the worst-case reservation strategy using EDF scheduling algorithm. It uses criticality-aware partitioning with first-fit allocation. For SPMC algorithm, we present the results for δ = 1 and δ = 4, where δ = 1 denotes the largest server period which has the least performance and lowest number of preemptions and δ ≤ 4 is considered to be the reasonable value of δ to maintain a low number of preemptions in the non-MC case [22].

div.head: A. Experiment Setup
div.p: Taskset generation: Our experiments are carried out using the task set generator proposed in [23]. The task parameters used in our generator are described as follows:
• m ∈{2, 4, 8} denotes the total number of processors.

• The minimum and maximum individual task utilization is given by u min (= 0.001) and u max (= 0.99) respectively. • P L ∈ [0.1, 0.2, . . . , 0.9] denotes the percentage of LC tasks in the system. • T i , the period of a task τ i is drawn uniformly at random from [10,100]. • The utilization values u L i and u H i are computed using the techniques proposed in [23] and [24]. • Execution budgets C L i and C H i are derived as u L i * T i and u H i * T i respectively. The total number of tasks in the system is lower bounded by m + 1 and upper bounded by 10 * m. We generate at least 10, 000 task sets for each value of total normalized utilization
div.formula: U B U B = max(U L H + U L L , U H H )
div.p: . For each such successfully generated task set we evaluate the performance of our scheduling algorithm with the existing algorithms.

div.head: B. Results
div.p: In Figure 2a, we compare the performance of SPMC against Semi-FP for m = 2 and P L = 0.5, where we plot the acceptance ratio (i.e., the fraction of schedulable task sets) of the algorithms versus total normalized utilization U B . As shown, the performance improvement of SPMC(δ = 1) and SPMC(δ = 4) over Semi-FP is as much as 12.7% and 24.3% respectively for U B = 0.8. As δ increases the performance of SPMC also increases but at the cost of increased number of preemptions. Further, to evaluate the loss in performance of the algorithms with respect to conventional MC scheduling algorithms (with no LC support) we also plot the acceptance ratio of the criticality-aware partitioned scheduling algorithms (EDF-VD [10] and AMC [18]) using UDP [21], the best performing allocation for these algorithms. As shown, the loss in schedulability between EDF-VD and SPMC is comparable to the loss in schedulability between AMC and Semi-FP.

In Figure 2b, we compare the percentage of additional LC utilization supported by SPMC over Semi-FP for m = 2. We present the results for three class of schedulable task sets -only by SPMC(δ = 1), only by Semi-FP and by both algorithms. Since both the algorithms offer 100% LC service after one mode switch we present the result for after two mode switch.When both processors switch to the HC mode SPMC(δ = 1) offers as much as 29.2% additional LC utilization compared to Semi-FP. Whereas, Semi-FP offers only as much as 17.6% additional LC utilization. This is due to the Semi-FP algorithm property of dropping all LC tasks in the processor that switched last to the HC mode. For those To evaluate the performance of the SPMC algorithm with respect to the percentage of LC tasks in a task set, we plot the weighted acceptance ratio (i.e., acceptance ratio weighted with U B ) of the algorithm for varying P L ∈ {0.1, . . . , 0.9} and m = {4, 8} in Figure 3. Weighted acceptance ratio is defined as
div.formula: W AR(S) = UB ∈S (AR(U B ) • U B ) UB ∈S U B
div.p: where S is the set of U B values and AR(U B ) is the acceptance ratio for a specific value of the system utilization U B . As shown, the performance of SPMC decreases initially and then increases with increasing number of LC tasks in a task set. The performance is high at the extremes as the task set comprises majorly of same criticality tasks. Due to the algorithm property of partitioning all the HC tasks first the performance is low when task set comprises both HC and LC tasks as these task sets are difficult to schedule using reservation for LC tasks.

To provide some insights on the performance gap between SPMC and WCR-EDF, we present the percentage of WCR-EDF infeasible task sets schedulable by the SPMC algorithm in Figure 4. As shown, for m = 4 and U B = 0.5, as much as 16.3% more task sets are deemed schedulable by SPMC(δ = 1) and as much as 72.6% more task sets are In Figure 5, we present the percentage of total LC utilization supported by the SPMC algorithm for varying number of mode switch. We plot the minimum guaranteed LC utilization for two different server periods (δ = 1 and δ = 4). As expected, the percentage of LC utilization supported decreases as the number of processors that switch to HC mode increases. The LC utilization decreases initially and remains the same as the number of mode switch increases. The reason is that once all the processors with migrating tasks switch to the HC mode there is no further decrease in the LC support as the remaining processors are composed of only non-migrating LC tasks.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, semi-partitioned mixed-criticality (SPMC) model to support LC tasks in the HC mode is investigated. We considered the problem of supporting full service after one mode switch. In the SPMC model, all the tasks are statically partitioned in the LC mode and upon mode switch, only the LC tasks are allowed to migrate between processors. We presented the scheduling strategy of the SPMC model and derived its utilization bound. Further, we compared the SPMC algorithm with the existing algorithm and our results show that SPMC has better performance in terms of both schedulability and LC support. In future work, we will generalize the analysis to include overheads and more than single deadline scaling factor; we also plan to extend the model to multi-criticality systems.
